forces.title: Global refining system under severe operational pressure
forces.description: The global refining system is experiencing significant operational stress, leading to demand destruction in some markets. This pressure is driven by major supply disruptions, including the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and an estimated 2 MMb/d of Russian refining capacity being offline. These factors directly impact crude availability and trade flows, necessitating complex and costly operational adjustments for refiners worldwide.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Efficiency losses from adapting to diverse crude grades
forces.description: Refiners are encountering efficiency losses and reduced product yields, particularly for high-demand products like jet fuel and diesel. This is a direct consequence of adapting their operations to process a broader and often sub-optimal range of crude oil grades due to global supply disruptions. This operational challenge elevates costs and diminishes the output of more valuable refined products.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Elevated refined product prices due to supply disruptions
forces.description: The combination of global refining disruptions and critically low refined product inventories has led to significantly higher prices for refined fuels globally. While higher prices may boost short-term revenues, they also indicate underlying system stress and can contribute to demand destruction if sustained, creating volatility and uncertainty for UK refiners' output markets.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Thin and fragmented global refined product inventories
forces.description: Refined product inventories are notably thinner and more fragmented by fuel type and location compared to crude oil stocks. This scarcity means that localized shortages can emerge rapidly, even if aggregate figures appear adequate, offering minimal buffer against sudden supply disruptions and increasing market volatility for specific products vital to the UK economy.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: Potential for strategic refined product inventory build-up
forces.description: The current energy crisis may prompt increased efforts to establish strategic reserves for refined products, mirroring the creation of crude oil inventories after the 1970s shocks. This could lead to new policy initiatives and investments aimed at enhancing refined product security and resilience for nations like the UK, creating opportunities for storage and logistics providers connected to refining.
forces.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

forces.title: UK industrial competitiveness eroded by high energy and carbon costs
forces.description: UK industrial energy prices are approximately 75% higher than the G7 average, compounded by significant carbon policy costs. This imbalance erodes the competitiveness of UK manufacturers, including those in the chemicals sector that rely on refinery outputs as feedstocks. This situation risks deindustrialisation and can reduce the domestic demand base for various refined products.

forces.title: Declining domestic production threatens UK midstream infrastructure
forces.description: The decline in UK Continental Shelf (UKCS) oil and gas production is jeopardizing the viability of critical midstream infrastructure (pipelines, processing facilities). Reduced throughput weakens asset economics, makes maintenance challenging, and risks accelerating rationalization, thereby increasing the UK's exposure to volatile global LNG markets and international price fluctuations. This also implies reduced domestic feedstock supply stability for refiners.

forces.title: Weak feedstock availability impacts broader UK industrial base
forces.description: Declining throughput and weaker feedstock availability, as evidenced by the closure of ExxonMobil’s Fife Ethylene Plant, illustrate the profound consequences for the UK's industrial competitiveness. Sustaining robust domestic oil and gas production is vital not only for upstream activity but also for maintaining the broader industrial base that relies on stable and affordable refinery-produced feedstocks for various manufacturing processes.

forces.title: Domestic North Sea production as a strategic feedstock source
forces.description: Domestic production from the North Sea is identified as a crucial source for much-needed energy and essential feedstocks (like naphtha, ethane, propane) for the UK's manufacturing sector. Maintaining this domestic supply base is seen as a key strategy to reduce exposure to import disruptions, manage transportation costs, and mitigate price volatility, thereby supporting the stability and competitiveness of UK refining operations and their downstream customers.

forces.title: UK's increasing reliance on imported energy for all needs
forces.description: The UK's domestic energy production is not keeping pace with demand, leading to over 40% of its energy needs being met by imports. This escalating import dependency amplifies the UK's vulnerability to volatile international commodity markets and geopolitical disruptions, which directly translates into higher and more unpredictable feedstock costs for domestic refiners, impacting their margins and operational stability.

viewpoints.title: Global refining system under severe stress, contributing to demand destruction
viewpoints.description: The global refining system is under significant stress due to major energy supply disruptions, notably the Strait of Hormuz closure and substantial Russian refining capacity being offline. This stress has contributed to demand destruction in certain markets. Refiners face challenges adapting to diverse crude grades, leading to efficiency losses and lower yields of high-demand products like jet fuel and diesel, despite some resulting in higher refined product prices. Overall, the operational health of the system is compromised.
viewpoints.source_title: Aftershocks: Energy security beyond the Strait of Hormuz crisis

viewpoints.title: Domestic North Sea production vital for UK industrial feedstock and refining
viewpoints.description: OEUK and the CIA emphasize the critical role of domestic North Sea oil and gas production in providing essential feedstocks, such as naphtha, ethane, and propane, for the UK's chemicals sector and broader manufacturing base. They argue that maintaining domestic supply reduces vulnerability to international market volatility, geopolitical risks, and high transport costs. Current policy trends, however, are accelerating the decline in domestic production, which negatively impacts the competitiveness of UK industries relying on refinery outputs.

demand_drivers.description: The UK's strategic chemicals sector, vital for pharmaceuticals, defence, energy, and automotive, requires substantial volumes of feedstocks like naphtha, ethane, and propane, which are direct outputs from oil and gas refining and processing. This creates a baseline demand for refinery products.

pnl_drivers.description: Declining domestic oil and gas production increases the UK's reliance on imported feedstocks for refining, exposing refiners to higher international price volatility, geopolitical risks, and increased transportation and logistics costs. This directly impacts the profitability and competitiveness of UK refining operations and the industries they supply.

market_sizing.methodology: Qualitative analysis of the UK chemical industry's reliance on refinery outputs (feedstocks) and the impact of domestic production trends on their competitiveness.
